According to the provided context, a class is a blueprint for a data type that combines data representation and methods for manipulating that data into one package. As stated, "a class is used to specify the form of an object and it combines data representation and methods for manipulating that data into one neat package" ([Source: Week4a_Classes and Objects.pptx]).

The data and functions within a class are called members of the class. A class definition starts with the keyword "class" followed by the class name, and the class body is enclosed by a pair of curly braces. For example, the class "Box" is defined as:

```cpp
class Box 
{    
    public: 
    double length; // Length of a box 
    double breadth; // Breadth of a box
    double height; // Height of a box 
} ;
```

An instance of a class is called an object. When a class is defined, no memory is allocated; memory is allocated when we create an object of a class. As mentioned, "An instance of a class is called an object. When a class is defined, no memory is allocated, we only define the specifications for its object. Memory is allocated when we create an object of a class" ([Source: Week4a_Classes and Objects.pptx]).

In the context of C++ programming, classes are the central feature that supports object-oriented programming and are often called user-defined types. When you define a class, you define a blueprint for a data type, and data members and member functions of a class can be used and accessed through objects of that class.

Classes in C++ are user-defined types that support object-oriented programming. They are used to specify the form of an object and combine data representation and methods for manipulating that data into one package. As stated in the context, "A class is used to specify the form of an object and it combines data representation and methods for manipulating that data into one neat package." 

The general syntax for defining a class is by using the keyword "class" followed by the class name and the class body, which is enclosed by a pair of curly braces. For example, "class Box { ... };". 

Classes have members, which include data and functions, and these members can be accessed by creating objects of the class. The context notes that "The data and functions within a class are called members of the class." 

Additionally, classes in C++ can have access specifiers, which define how the members of a class can be accessed. There are three access specifiers in C++: public, private, and protected. The public access specifier, for instance, makes the class members accessible from any part of the program. As mentioned in the context, "The Public members are accessible from any part of program." 

Overall, classes are a fundamental concept in C++ programming, allowing for the creation of custom data types and the organization of code in a logical and structured way.

According to the provided context, classes and objects are fundamental concepts in C++ programming. 

A class is defined as "a blueprint for a data type" that "specifies the form of an object" and "combines data representation and methods for manipulating that data into one neat package" ([Source: Week4a_Classes and Objects.pptx]). It is a user-defined type that supports object-oriented programming.

An object, on the other hand, is "an instance of a class" ([Source: Week4a_Classes and Objects.pptx]). When a class is defined, no memory is allocated, but memory is allocated when an object of the class is created. Objects can be used to access and manipulate the data members and member functions of a class.

In simpler terms, a class is like a template or a design pattern, while an object is an actual instance of that template, with its own set of attributes (data) and methods (functions). As stated in the context, "we can create multiple objects of a class" using the syntax "ClassName ObjectName;" ([Source: Week4a_Classes and Objects.pptx]). 

For example, in the provided context, a class "Box" is defined with public members such as length, breadth, and height. An object of this class can be created to access and manipulate these members.

Based on the provided context, an exception refers to an unexpected condition in a program that causes an error, leading to the program's failure. 

According to the context: "Exception refers to unexpected condition in a program. The unusual conditions could be faults, Causing an error which in turn causes the program to fail." (Section 3: Exceptions)

Additionally, exceptions can be categorized into two types: synchronous and asynchronous. 

Synchronous exceptions occur during program execution due to input data faults or unsuitable techniques, whereas asynchronous exceptions are caused by events or faults beyond the program's control. 

(Section 4: Types of Exceptions)
